title: Building financial resilience: Five developments shaping EU stress testing
gist: Oxford Economics argues EU bank stress testing is shifting from siloed macro, climate and ESG exercises to a single integrated framework, with the EBA's draft 2027 EU-wide stress test set to impose transition and physical climate shocks simultaneously with core macro-financial shocks on the largest institutions, and nature-related risk climbing the supervisory agenda for all EU banks. Note: the raw record lists Duncan Campbell as author, while the article text is bylined to Daniel Moseley (Associate Director, Scenarios and Macro Modeling) and Robert Marks (Lead Economist).

insights.claim: Under the EBA's draft EU-wide stress test for 2027, mandated for the largest financial institutions, transition and physical climate risk must be incorporated as simultaneous shocks alongside the core macro-financial shocks rather than as a separate exercise.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A hard 2027 deadline creates a near-term compliance spend cycle for large EU banks and a revenue window for scenario/model vendors; watch which banks disclose combined-shock capital impacts first.
insights.quote: under the EBA’s draft EU-wide stress test for 2027, which will be mandated for the largest financial institutions, transition and physical climate risk should be incorporated in the exercise as simultaneous shocks alongside the core macro-financial shocks

insights.claim: The EBA's guidelines on environmental scenario analysis extend the requirement beyond systemic banks: all EU banks are expected to run climate and nature-related scenarios on the most material risks they face.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: The addressable market for environmental scenario data and modelling widens from a handful of G-SIBs to the entire EU banking system, including mid-caps with no in-house capability.
insights.quote: all EU banks, under the EBA’s guidelines on environmental scenario analysis, are expected to conduct climate and nature-related scenarios on the most material risks their institution faces

insights.claim: Climate and environmental stress tests are transitioning from exploratory exercises into a core input to bank capital adequacy processes as regulators begin to mandate them.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Once climate feeds capital, it stops being a disclosure cost and starts affecting lending capacity and pricing for carbon- and hazard-exposed borrowers.
insights.quote: climate and environmental stress tests are moving from exploratory towards becoming a core part of banks capital adequacy process
insights.locator: Financial institutions are facing an evolving

insights.claim: Macroeconomic stress testing, climate scenario analysis and environmental risk assessment have historically been run as separate exercises with different assumptions, datasets and methodologies, and that separation is becoming increasingly difficult to justify to supervisors.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Banks running three disconnected risk stacks face consolidation costs and model-validation risk; vendors offering one coherent framework gain share over point solutions.
insights.quote: Historically, macroeconomic stress testing, climate scenario analysis and environmental risk assessments have been conducted as separate exercises using different assumptions, datasets and methodologies.
insights.locator: 1. Build a more integrated view of risk

insights.claim: Oxford Economics states its own baseline global forecast now embeds forward-looking transition and physical climate risks, meaning climate is no longer an overlay on a climate-neutral central case.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: If mainstream macro forecasters embed climate in the baseline, consensus growth and inflation paths themselves start carrying a climate drag that markets may not have priced separately.
insights.quote: Our baseline forecast at Oxford Economics now embeds our view on both forward-looking transition and physical climate risks across the global economy.
insights.locator: 1. Build a more integrated view of risk

insights.claim: Firms are expected to model how shocks cascade through the economy, financial system and environment in both central and adverse scenarios, rather than treating each risk as an independent threat.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Correlated-shock modelling typically produces fatter tails than siloed testing, so expect stress-test losses to come in worse than legacy exercises implied.
insights.locator: 1. Build a more integrated view of risk

themes.theme: Traceability as the new supervisory bar

insights.claim: Producing a severe but plausible scenario is no longer sufficient; supervisors expect institutions to demonstrate the full transmission path from the initial macro shock through sectors, borrowers and portfolios with internally consistent assumptions for GDP, inflation, rates, sector output and asset prices.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Audit-trail requirements favour structural macro models over reduced-form or black-box ML approaches in regulated risk stacks.
insights.quote: Creating severe but plausible scenarios is no longer enough.
insights.locator: 2. Connect every scenario to real business impacts

insights.claim: Traceability is becoming as important as the scenario itself, with the worked example being the chain from rising carbon prices to higher inflation to interest rate decisions.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: The carbon-price-to-inflation-to-policy-rate channel becoming a standard regulatory scenario is an argument that carbon pricing tightening is a rates risk, not just an equity sector risk.
insights.quote: For example, understanding the chain of events from the rise of carbon prices to higher inflation to interest rate decisions.
insights.locator: 2. Connect every scenario to real business impacts

insights.claim: Oxford Economics positions its Global Economic Model (GEM) as the single framework linking macro conditions, sector dynamics, climate transition, physical climate impacts and nature risk with transparent transmission channels.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Names the specific commercial toolset banks may license to meet the 2027 requirement; useful as a competitive marker for other scenario-data providers.

insights.claim: Supervisors expect transition and physical climate risk to feed directly into core credit risk parameters — probability of default, loss given default, expected losses and ultimately capital planning — rather than sitting in a separate ESG workstream.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Climate feeding PD/LGD mechanically raises risk-weighted assets on exposed loan books, which is a direct hit to capital ratios and dividend capacity, not a disclosure line item.
insights.quote: Supervisors increasingly expect both transition and physical climate risks to feed directly into core credit risk models, influencing probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD), expected losses and ultimately capital planning.
insights.locator: 3. Treat climate risk as core to business strategy

insights.claim: Physical climate risk splits into two distinct financial channels: acute events such as floods, storms and heatwaves that disrupt businesses and impair collateral values immediately, and chronic changes such as rising temperatures and water stress that erode productivity and long-run growth.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: The acute channel hits collateral and insurance; the chronic channel hits terminal growth assumptions — they require different hedges and show up in different parts of a valuation.
insights.quote: Acute events such as floods, storms and heatwaves cause immediate disruption to businesses and collateral values, while gradual chronic changes, including rising temperatures and water stress, steadily erode productivity and long-term economic growth.
insights.locator: 3. Treat climate risk as core to business strategy

insights.claim: Headline GDP forecasts are explicitly declared insufficient for stress testing, with the direction of travel toward sector-, region- and supply-chain-level granularity so that institutions can attribute losses to sector exposure, geographic concentration or macro conditions.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Demand shifts toward granular sector and geospatial datasets and away from headline macro subscriptions; also implies bank loan-book disclosure gets more sector-specific.
insights.quote: Headline GDP forecasts are no longer sufficient, and more granularity is the direction of travel.
insights.locator: 4. Understand risk where it really sits

insights.claim: Construction, agriculture, manufacturing, utilities and transport are identified as facing materially different vulnerabilities to transition versus physical climate risk, so climate exposure cannot be assessed at the aggregate portfolio level.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: These five sectors are the likely first movers in stressed-capital repricing of credit; screen lenders by their concentration in them.
insights.quote: sectors such as construction, agriculture, manufacturing, utilities and transport all face different vulnerabilities to both transition and physical climate risks
insights.locator: 4. Understand risk where it really sits

insights.claim: A practical bottleneck to granular stress testing is consistent mapping between counterparties, industries and regulatory reporting classifications, which requires robust sector-level data infrastructure rather than better models.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: The binding constraint is data plumbing, so value accrues to counterparty-mapping and classification data vendors as much as to scenario modellers.
insights.locator: 4. Understand risk where it really sits

themes.theme: Nature risk as the next frontier

insights.claim: Nature-related physical risk propagates well beyond agriculture: deterioration of ecosystem services such as water supply, soil quality regulation, biomass provisioning and pollination transmits through supply chains into manufacturing, construction, utilities and food production.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Nature exposure is a supply-chain dependency question, not a land-ownership question, so screening only agri names understates portfolio exposure.
insights.quote: the economic impacts focussed on primary sectors but also extending well beyond agriculture, affecting manufacturing, construction, utilities, food and food production via supply chains

insights.claim: Nature transition risk will arrive through concrete policy instruments named as land-use restrictions, pollution taxes, water quotas and recycling mandates, mirroring how carbon pricing created transition risk for emitters.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Gives a watchlist of specific regulatory levers to track for input-cost shocks in water-intensive, land-intensive and packaging-heavy businesses.
insights.quote: Land-use restrictions, pollution taxes, water quotas and recycling mandates are just some of the transition risks portfolios are exposed to.

insights.claim: Nature stress-testing methodology is still evolving but is judged workable today: it begins with screening and materiality tests to identify main risk drivers and mostly relies on geospatial data on the state of nature and ecosystem condition, borrowing commonalities from climate stress testing.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Geospatial ecosystem-condition data becomes a required input for EU banks, a narrow niche with few incumbent suppliers.
insights.quote: While methodologies are still evolving, there are sufficient data and tools to get started.

insights.claim: The article's closing position is that nature risk has already become a material driver of financial risk that institutions can no longer ignore, framing the whole shift as moving beyond compliance to resilience in a world of increasingly correlated risks.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Signals that nature follows the same regulatory adoption curve climate did roughly five years earlier; early positioning in nature-data capability is the analogue trade.
insights.quote: Nature risk is becoming a material driver of financial risk that institutions can no longer ignore.
